title: Psalm 122: Pray for the Peace of Jerusalem
summary: A pilgrim remembers the joy of being invited to go up to the house of the LORD and now stands inside Jerusalem's gates. He praises the city as the place where Israel's tribes gather to give thanks and where the thrones of David's house give justice, then calls for prayer for Jerusalem's peace and commits himself to seek its good for the sake of his people and of God's house.
story: Psalm 121 set the pilgrim on the road with the hills ahead. Psalm 122 brings him to the goal: “Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem.” The Songs of Ascents move from the distant exile of Psalm 120 toward Zion, and this is the first psalm in the collection set inside the city. What the pilgrim finds there is more than a building. Jerusalem is where the scattered tribes become one people before God, where the king's justice is supposed to be found, and where peace ought to live. The psalm ends not with arrival but with a responsibility: the pilgrim will pray for and work for the city's good. Later Songs of Ascents return to Zion again and again (Psalms 125, 126, 128, 129, 132, 133, 134).
historical:
The heading reads “A song of ascents. Of David.” The Hebrew phrase translated “Of David” (ledavid) can mean written by David, belonging to a Davidic collection, dedicated to David, or written in David's manner, and scholars weigh it differently. The attributions in the headings of the Songs of Ascents are also not uniform across ancient manuscripts and translations, which leads some to see them as later additions. Readers who accept Davidic authorship note that David made Jerusalem his capital, brought the ark there, and planned the temple, and that the tabernacle could itself be called the house of the LORD (1 Samuel 1:7 uses that language for the sanctuary at Shiloh). Many scholars instead date the psalm later, after Solomon built the temple, or after the exile, pointing to the picture of tribes going up by established custom and to the reference to thrones of the house of David, which may look back on the dynasty. The psalm fits any period when pilgrims came to a standing temple.

The tribes going up “as a testimony for Israel” refers to the law's command that Israel appear before the LORD at the three pilgrim festivals (Exodus 23:17; Deuteronomy 16:16). After the northern tribes broke away under Jeroboam around 930 BC, he set up rival shrines at Bethel and Dan to keep his people from going up to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26-29). A psalm that pictures all the tribes gathering in one city speaks either of the united kingdom or of the hope that Israel would one day be whole again.
cultural:
An ancient city's gates were more than doors. They were thick-walled chambers where elders sat, trade happened, and cases were heard, and the king or his officials gave judgment near them (2 Samuel 15:2 shows Absalom intercepting people coming to the king for judgment at the gate). The thrones of judgment in verse 5 reflect that role. In Israel the king was meant to be the final court of appeal and the protector of the weak, as Solomon's famous judgment between two mothers shows (1 Kings 3:16-28). Jerusalem was therefore the center of both worship and justice, and the psalm holds them together.

The description of Jerusalem “built up as a city united together” may describe its compact layout on a narrow ridge, closely packed within its walls, or it may describe the unity of the people it gathered. For a pilgrim from a farming village, the sight of the walls, towers, and fortresses of verse 7 would have been overwhelming. The city's size and strength made its peace all the more precious and all the more fragile, as its later sieges would show.
literary: The psalm moves in three stages: joy at the invitation and arrival (verses 1-2), praise of the city (verses 3-5), and prayer for its peace (verses 6-9). It is full of wordplay that English cannot keep. The city's name, Yerushalayim, was heard in Israel as related to shalom, peace, and the psalm plays on it: verse 6 in Hebrew runs sha'alu shelom Yerushalayim, ask for the peace of Jerusalem, followed by a prayer that those who love her will prosper (yishlayu), and verse 7 adds peace (shalom) and prosperity (shalvah). The sounds sh and l echo through the lines. The word “house” frames the whole: it opens with “the house of the LORD” in verse 1 and closes with “the house of the LORD our God” in verse 9, with the house of David between them in verse 5.

outline.t: Glad at the call to go up; standing in the gates
Jerusalem: where the tribes give thanks and justice sits
A call to pray for the city's peace
Seeking the city's good for others' sake

doctrines.note: Jerusalem is where scattered tribes become one worshiping people, going up together “to give thanks to the name of the LORD.” The psalm treats gathered worship as a gift and a joy, not a burden, and it ties love for God's house to love for the brothers and friends who share it.

The pilgrim is told to pray for the city, and he does, turning his own blessing outward. Intercession here is practical and public: peace within walls, security in fortresses, prosperity for those who love the place.
Worship and justice sit side by side in the city: the house of the LORD and the thrones of the house of David. God's rule is meant to be seen in right judgment as well as right praise.

words.note: Shalom, peace. The word means much more than the absence of war: wholeness, well-being, right relationship, everything as it should be. It appears three times here and is woven into the sound of the city's name. To pray for Jerusalem's shalom is to pray for the full flourishing of the place where God meets his people.

Alah, to go up. It is the verb behind the whole collection's title (the noun ma'alah, ascent, comes from the same root) and the ordinary word for traveling to Jerusalem, which stands high in the hills. The tribes “go up” in verse 4, and the verb carries both a physical climb and the sense of approaching God.

Samach, to rejoice or be glad. The psalm opens with gladness at an invitation, before the pilgrim has even arrived. The same verb describes the joy commanded at Israel's festivals (Deuteronomy 16:14-15), where worship was meant to be a feast.

christ: Jesus himself went up to Jerusalem for the festivals, from the Passover trip at twelve (Luke 2:41-42) to the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:10) and his last Passover. As he came near the city for the last time, he wept over it and said it had not known the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41-42), a sorrowful echo of this psalm's prayer. In him the functions the psalm gives to Jerusalem come together: he is the true temple where God dwells with people (John 2:19-21) and the son of David who sits on the throne of judgment. The New Testament then speaks of a heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the living God to which believers have already come (Hebrews 12:22) and which Paul calls free and our mother (Galatians 4:26). This is a fulfillment by enlargement, not by allegory: the gathering of tribes in one city widens into a gathering of every nation in Christ.

hard.q: What does praying for the peace of Jerusalem mean for Christians now?
hard.a: The phrase is often quoted in debates about the modern city and state, so the question matters. Some Christians read the psalm as calling for ongoing prayer for the literal city of Jerusalem and the Jewish people, since the city remains central in Scripture's hopes. Others read the psalm's Jerusalem as fulfilled in Christ and his people, the heavenly Jerusalem of Hebrews 12, and apply it chiefly to prayer for the church and for peace among all peoples. Many hold both together. In its own setting the psalm is a pilgrim's prayer for the city of the temple and the Davidic throne, and it asks for shalom, which includes justice (verse 5) and the good of neighbors (verse 8). Whatever application a reader draws, the psalm's own terms rule out using its words to bless hostility or injustice.

questions: The pilgrim is glad before he arrives, just at being invited. What makes gathered worship feel like gladness, or like duty, for you?
Jerusalem was a place of both worship and justice. Why might God want those two things to live in the same place, and what happens when they are separated?
Verse 8 says the pilgrim prays for the city's peace for the sake of his brothers and friends. For whose sake could you seek the peace of the place where you live?
